headline: Medium risk: shared MCP and write-capable agentic-flow can leak or corrupt work when paired with broad-network Haystack, but no direct evidence of default cross-agent trust.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP, stdin/stdout, and shell-like tooling, while agent_b also uses MCP servers. That creates a plausible instruction-smuggling path if B’s outputs are fed into A or vice versa. No direct shared channel is documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF the orchestrator routes agent_b text into agent_a prompts or MCP inputs
IF either agent parses the other’s output as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic prompt chaining between agents
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent messages
Require a human review step before MCP tool calls
Strip executable-looking blocks from exchanged text
requires-engineering: isolate agents with separate message buses

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and secrets (Ed25519 signatures), and can egress over allowlisted network paths; agent_b has broad network egress and REST/MCP access. Even without a shared filesystem, the pair can move sensitive content outward through normal outputs or API calls.
conditions: IF agent_a is given secrets or repository content that agent_b can query or summarize
IF either agent forwards prompts, files, or retrieved context to external APIs
mitigations: Remove secrets from agent_a inputs
Restrict agent_b to non-sensitive corpora
Turn off network egress for one agent during sensitive runs
Log and review all outbound payloads
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can execute shell commands, modify git state, install packages, and spawn subprocesses; agent_b can also use MCP and broad network egress. Overlap on mutable resources is plausible, but no shared writable directory or locking model is documented, so the conflict is real but not proven high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository checkout
IF both can write to the same git worktree or MCP-backed resource without locks
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Serialize git writes through one coordinator
Disable package installation in one agent
Use per-agent MCP endpoints
requires-engineering: add file and git locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can generate analysis and modify repository state, while agent_b is a search/RAG system that may consume upstream outputs. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream retrieval or actions. The profiles do not prove blind trust, so medium is the safest supported level.
conditions: IF agent_b ingests agent_a output without verification
IF downstream automation acts on B’s synthesized results
mitigations: Require citations for all A-to-B handoffs
Add a verification step before B acts
Limit A to draft-only outputs
Have B cross-check against source documents
requires-engineering: implement confidence gating between agents

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles code, repository metadata, and task prompts, while agent_b only lists anonymous usage statistics. No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented, so compliance risk is limited to a small, plausible gap rather than a confirmed breach. The other agent is cited because the pairwise flow is the concern.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into agent_a or agent_b workflows
IF retention or residency policies differ for the same dataset
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair
Document retention settings for both agents
Review vendor DPAs before deployment
Separate datasets by compliance class
requires-engineering: add policy-based routing
